h1: Careers in non-alcoholic and low-alcohol drinks
title: Careers in Non-Alcoholic Drinks | Craft Beer School
desc: Roles in non-alcoholic and low-alcohol beer and drinks: brewer, process technologist, quality, product developer, sales and brand.
teaser: Non-alcoholic beer needs real brewing skill. Here are the roles and the skills behind them.
standfirst: The market for no- and low-alcohol drinks has made room for new jobs. This guide describes the roles and what each asks of you.
sections: Why the field needs skilled people

Taking alcohol out of beer, or never making it, changes the whole product. Alcohol carries flavour and body. It protects beer from microbes. Remove it and a brewer has to rebuild mouthfeel and keep the beer stable. That takes process knowledge, not a shortcut.

The definitions also differ: some countries use a limit at or near zero, others allow up to 0.5 % ABV. A technologist has to know the rules where the beer is sold.

Many plants that make non-alcoholic beer also make other no- and low-alcohol drinks, such as kombucha, hop water or fermented soft drinks. Skills carry across if you understand fermentation and stability.

Some brewers make non-alcoholic beer by limited fermentation. Others brew a normal beer and remove the alcohol by vacuum distillation or membrane filtration. Either method needs control of temperature, pressure and timing. The person in this role watches flavour loss, oxygen pick-up and microbial risk.

Entry is through general brewing skills. See how to become a brewer without a brewing degree.

Equipment cost shapes the field. A craft brewer without a dealcoholisation unit may use contract facilities that offer this as a service. Learn what each method needs before you pitch an idea.

Plant hygiene and cleaning schedules also matter more in low-alcohol production, because the beer has less natural protection against contamination.

Non-alcoholic beer is more at risk from spoilage than regular beer. Quality technicians plan sampling, run microbiology checks and test shelf life. Pasteurisation or sterile filtration is common. If you like lab work and detail, this role suits you.

Know how to taste for faults and how to document findings. Beer off-flavours is a good start.

A technologist will also check packaging: oxygen at fill, seals and storage temperature in transit, all of which affect shelf life more than usual. A shelf-life trial that runs warm and cold is standard practice.

Developers write the brief, run trial batches, taste with panels and work out costs. A product developer in this space also researches the customer: someone who is driving, training, avoiding alcohol for personal reasons or simply drinking less. Good developers bring both creativity and discipline.

Clear records keep a trial from becoming a guess. Learn to design a simple test, change one variable at a time and note the result.

Testing with a panel matters here. Alcohol hides faults in regular beer. Without it a worty, sweet or thin character is exposed. Use spit cups for large panels and offer water between samples.

The category is young in many markets, so teams explain what the product is and why it tastes the way it does. A sales or brand role asks for good storytelling, honest claims and knowledge of local rules on labelling. Health claims are usually off limits.

See working in beer sales for how a sales role works.

Be careful with claims in copy. Do not say the product is healthy. Do not call it a replacement for alcohol in a way that suggests a medical benefit. Say what it is, how it tastes and how it is made.

Learn brewing basics first, then study non-alcoholic methods. Taste widely and keep notes. Ask producers for a visit. We do not quote salaries or promise jobs. Pay and demand differ by country and employer.

Look at both ends of the market: small craft producers that make one or two non-alcoholic beers and large brewers with dedicated lines.

Follow industry news and trade shows in your region. Producers talk openly about methods and problems at events. A polite question gets a useful answer.

If you want to see whether you enjoy the technical side, learn how the main methods work and what they do to flavour. Our Non-Alcoholic Beer course is a two-week live online programme that covers methods, stability and flavour. It is a gentle way to find out where you fit before you commit to a career change.

Notice who else is in your class. Others on a short course may work in drinks production or retail. Their stories show how the same product looks from the shop floor.
faqs: Do I need a brewing background?
It helps, since non-alcoholic beer builds on normal brewing, but sales and brand roles do not require it.
Is non-alcoholic beer a safe career bet?
Demand differs by country and changes. Build transferable skills.
The legal limit differs by country. Check the local definition.
Can I work in this field if I do not drink?
Yes. Many roles rely on process knowledge and structured tasting. Spit cups let you taste without swallowing.
